title: The Quiet Garden
strapline: A slow, gentle patch of outdoors — for lying under leaves, watching clouds and letting the day go soft.
intent: Children discover that being outdoors can be still and restful, not only fast and loud — nature as a calming force.
Children practise unhurried noticing — birdsong, swaying branches, the warmth of the sun — settling body and mind.
Children who overload in a busy playground get an outdoor retreat that's peaceful rather than stimulating.
Children build a felt connection with the natural world and a sense of wellbeing that comes from being in it.
Children experience awe and wonder at small, slow things — a floating cloud, a ladybird, a falling petal.
implementation: Set aside a sheltered, softly planted corner away from the wheeled-toy racetrack — grasses, scented plants, a shady tree, somewhere to lie down.
Offer low, restful invitations: a picnic rug, cushions, a hammock or slung fabric, a basket of blankets to burrow into.
Keep it gently resourced — a nature-spotting card, a magnifier, a wind chime — not stuffed with busy toys.
Model slowness: lie back with the children, watch the clouds, whisper about what you can hear, and let silences sit.
Protect the calm — small numbers, a quiet-voices understanding — so it stays a genuine retreat within the garden.
Use every season: bare branches and frost, blossom, warm grass, crunchy leaves — the quiet garden changes but always slows you down.
key_questions: What can you hear if we lie very still?
What shapes can you see in the clouds?
How does the breeze feel on your face?
What tiny thing can you find near you?
Does your body feel calm out here?

impact.text: Children notice the world — wind, leaves, birds, clouds — with fascination and calm.
Children regulate big feelings, using the quiet outdoors as a place that settles them.
Children begin to know what their body needs — rest, calm, fresh air — and do something about it.
Children ask real questions about the natural world and expect real answers.
Children treat living things gently — a ladybird, a plant — as a matter of course.

enhancements: A sound garden of soft wind chimes, bamboo and rustling grasses to listen to.
A cloud-watching basket of blankets and a laminated 'what can you see?' card.
Scented planting — lavender, mint, rosemary — to brush and smell for calm.
A bird feeder in view, with a spotting card, for gentle patient watching.
A baby version: a shaded blanket under a tree with dappled light and hanging natural mobiles.

playing_exploring: Children explore nature slowly and with all their senses, following what draws them.
The calm space invites open, unhurried wondering rather than busy activity.
active_learning: Children learn that the quiet garden settles them and choose to go there when they need calm.
Sustained, peaceful attention to small natural things deepens over repeated visits.
creating_thinking: Children notice patterns and changes in nature and ask their own questions.
They make connections between weather, seasons and how the garden feels and looks.
